f1a: Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening, though it can be a bit of a backseat driver. Sometimes it really did see the truck you missed, like when you're about to take on way more than you can handle, or someone's about to cross a line with you. Other times it's yelling about trucks that aren't there. You can hear it out and keep your hands on the wheel. With most decisions there's room to find out which it was. I'd weigh what it's saying against what you already know, like how this has gone before, and then notice what really happens. If it might be danger right now, though, or something in your body a doctor should look at, I'd get some distance or get checked first, and find out how right it was later.
f1b: Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening. A lot of the time it's a part of you that's trying to protect you, making a guess about what's coming: that you'll get overwhelmed, maybe, or that people will laugh at you. It can be right! It can also be scared of things that never happen, so I'd hear it out and then decide for myself. With most choices, I'd write down what it predicted and look again afterward. Did they really laugh? If it might be danger right now, though, or something in your body a doctor should look at, I'd get some distance or get checked first, and find out how right it was later.
d1: Leaving it for later doesn't mean giving up on your little one. It's more like lowering the dose of something strong. Unless what you don't want is the whole inner-child idea. Then it isn't a pacing problem at all, and I'd drop the language and leave it dropped (no sneaking it back in as a "gentler" exercise, or calling the dishes reparenting). Looking after yourself and keeping yourself safe can go on in whatever words fit you. So can figuring out where you're headed, and getting support from people.
d2: If you do want the relationship and it's the depth that's too much, start with whether you can get out. If you're not sure you could stop and come back if you needed to, or you keep losing track of where you are, I'd set the inward exercises aside for now and come back out to the room first. Same if going inward is itself making it worse. I wouldn't try another inward technique to prove you're able to take it. Once you're steadier, there's a harm-reduction saying that fits here: start low and go slow. Low might be something protective you do out in your life, or time with somebody who's good for you. Or just a short hello to your little one, eyes open, before any imagery.
d3: A full pause is the last resort, though you might need one for safety whether you want it or not. If it comes to that, I'd write down what made it necessary, and the last level that was really workable. Then what you'd need to see change, plus your own OK, before going back. After a while you'll probably catch yourself thinking, "Maybe just a quick hello would be okay?" I'd wait on that too, until the change is there. Taking care of yourself, and seeing people who are good for you, can keep going. If you never checked how an earlier hard session left you (your sleep, the days after), do that in the meantime. And when you do come back, start at that last workable level, or below it.
p1: Whatever you try from that map, I wouldn't go by how pleasant a session felt to tell whether it was good for you. This kind of work can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes hard dreams, or stuff you'd rather never have met. A session can also be really intense and get you nowhere. Even staying present the whole time doesn't tell you enough by itself. It's a bit like the gym, where sore and injured can feel pretty similar that evening, and it's the next few days that tell you which one it was.
p2: What I'd look at instead is whether you could have stopped and come back to the room if you'd wanted to. Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is everything in you saying no? And how have you been sleeping, and getting through your days since? If you don't know yet, give it some time before you call it healing or harm. While you're still finding your level, I'd make it easier one thing at a time (shorter, or with your eyes open), so you learn what made the difference. If it's getting worse, change several things at once, and have someone steady with you for the next one.
p3: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. If you're not sure yet whether you want to, you can wait. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. Those dreams and images that come up can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.
c2: And being yourself with people doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller things you tell them, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you're still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I'd either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn't safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing, maybe even like falling in love. A lot of that is relief, though, after going so long without it. Whether you're good for each other, and whether they can be trusted with more of you, takes longer to find out.
i1: If being alone is part of what hurt you, reaching toward people can be one of the ways the grown-up you looks after your little one. If you like the word, call it reparenting. A decent parent wouldn't tell a lonely child to become totally self-sufficient before they're allowed to see their friends. So sometimes the grown-up move is picking up the phone, or setting up the visit. Or asking a social worker what's out there, or just getting yourself through the door of a room where people share something real.
i2: I wouldn't put all my eggs in one basket here, either. Some of the baskets might be people you already trust, especially the friendships that go both ways. Others could be a peer-support group. Or a church or a sangha, if one really fits you. A class works too, or volunteering. So does a therapist. Not every one has to work out, and none of it means dropping somebody who's good for you. I'd bring the Protector along for this part, though. A high-control group can make you feel like you belong, and so can somebody in charge who uses people.
